Impedance control [@hogan1985impedance] frames contact as neither pure position nor pure force control. The environment behaves as an admittance, accepting force and yielding motion, so the manipulator is controlled as an impedance, accepting motion deviations and generating compliant force ($F = Z(v)$). The joint's drive controller converts position setpoints into a **virtual spring-damper system**\index{Virtual spring-damper system!definition}:
$$F_{\text{contact}} = K_p (x_{\text{des}} - x) + K_d (\dot{x}_{\text{des}} - \dot{x})$$
The joint's programmed stiffness $K_p$ and damping $K_d$ make it yield under position error. This can reduce contact loading, but the response still depends on actuator bandwidth, saturation, and contact dynamics; the equation alone does not cap impact force. The allowable approach speed must therefore come from the qualified contact response.
:::

::: {#fig-02-real-strain-wave-gear fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Strain wave gear assembly**: Robotic strain wave transmission component set: (1) elliptical wave generator with flexible ball bearings, (2) flexible cup flexspline with external teeth, (3) rigid circular spline with internal teeth, and (4) transmission systems invariant governing reflected rotor inertia ($J_{\text{ref}} = N^2 J_{\text{rotor}}$). Elastic deformation enables zero initial backlash at high reduction ratios ($50:1$ to $160:1$), but introduces torsional compliance, hysteresis, and tooth fatigue vulnerability under sudden shock loads." fig-alt="Annotated component set of a robotic strain wave gear transmission, highlighting the wave generator, flexspline, circular spline, and reflected inertia invariant."}
![](images/jpg/fig02_real_strain_wave_gear_annotated.jpg){width="70%"}
:::

The strain wave assembly in @fig-02-real-strain-wave-gear obtains its reduction through repeated elastic deformation of the flexspline. That compliance allows the motor and link to move differently under load, so motor-side tracking alone cannot establish the output motion.

::: {#fig-02-real-broken-gear-tooth fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Gear tooth shock fracture under high reflected inertia**: Macro-fracture of a high-torque transmission gear tooth undergoing cyclic stress testing at NASA Glenn Research Center: [①] intact gear tooth flank supporting continuous drive contact; [②] tooth root fillet stress concentration, where cyclic tension initiates micro-cracking; [③] sheared tooth fragment with granular fatigue striations and sudden cleavage fracture under shock load; and [④] reflected rotor inertia ($J_{\text{ref}} = N^2 J_{\text{rotor}}$). A high gear ratio reduces backdrivability and can increase tooth-root stress under impact; compliance and the contact path determine how much energy reaches any one tooth." fig-alt="Annotated macro photograph of a fractured transmission gear tooth, identifying the intact flank, the root fillet crack initiation site, the sheared tooth fragment with granular cleavage surface, and the reflected rotor inertia formula."}
![](images/jpg/fig02_real_broken_gear_tooth_annotated.jpg){width="65%"}
:::

The damaged tooth in @fig-02-real-broken-gear-tooth illustrates why repeated contact loads belong in actuator qualification. A transmission that meets static torque requirements may still accumulate damage under reversals and impacts. Smooth proposals reduce excitation, but their admissibility still depends on measured output response and the qualified load envelope.

### Actuation regimes and gear reduction trade-offs {#sec-body-actuation-regimes}

The choice of transmission trades continuous torque density against mechanical backdrivability. Gearboxes amplify motor torque linearly by $N_g$ ($\tau_{\text{out}} = \eta N_g \tau_{\text{motor}}$), but amplify the rotor's rotational inertia quadratically by $N_g^2$ ($J_{\text{ref}} = N_g^2 J_{\text{rotor}}$). This fundamental scaling asymmetry divides robotic actuation into three distinct architectural regimes (@tbl-02-mechanical-drives):

| Transmission                       | Gear Ratio ($N$)                     | Reflected Inertia ($N^2$)                 | Implication for Learned Policies                                                                                                        |
|:-----------------------------------|:-------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Quasi-Direct Drive (QDD)**       | $3:1\text{--}10:1$ ($N \le 10$)      | $N^2 \le 100$ (Low)                       | Lower reflected inertia supports backdriving and current-based torque estimation; contact response still requires qualification.        |
| **Planetary Gearing (Multistage)** | $15:1\text{--}50:1$ ($N \approx 30$) | $N^2 \approx 225\text{--}2500$ (Moderate) | Semi-backdrivable; higher torque density than QDD; gear tooth backlash ($5\text{--}15\text{ arcmin}$) requires load-side joint sensing. |
| **Strain Wave (Harmonic Drive)**   | $50:1\text{--}160:1$ ($N \ge 50$)    | $N^2 \ge 2500\text{--}25{,}600$ (Extreme) | High reflected inertia; zero initial backlash; torsional compliance and impact loading require qualification.                           |

: **Actuator transmission trade-off**: Reduction ratio ($N$), reflected rotor inertia scaling ($N^2$), and the consequence for learned control policies across Quasi-Direct Drive, multi-stage planetary, and strain wave transmissions. {#tbl-02-mechanical-drives tbl-colwidths="[22,18,20,40]"}

Transmission choice must satisfy both the torque requirement and the permitted contact response. Direct drive removes gearbox backlash but requires a motor large enough to supply the output torque itself [@asada1983design]. Reduction allows a smaller motor to deliver the same torque while adding reflected inertia and transmission losses. Backdrivability describes whether an external force at the output can move the motor through that transmission. The simplified reverse-drive relation is:
$$\tau_{\text{ext}} = \frac{N^2 J_{\text{rotor}}}{\eta_{\text{rev}}} \ddot{q} + \frac{\tau_{\text{friction}}}{\eta_{\text{rev}}}$$
where $\eta_{\text{rev}}$ is reverse transmission efficiency. Low reverse efficiency raises the required external torque, while reflected inertia raises the torque needed for rapid acceleration. A high ratio can therefore resist contact motion strongly, but backdrivability must be characterized on the assembly rather than inferred from ratio alone.

**Quasi-direct drive (QDD)** actuation[^fn-hist-qdd-lineage] uses a high-torque motor with a low reduction ratio [@seok2015design; @wensing2017proprioceptive; @katz2019mini]. Reducing the reflected inertia and transmission friction improves mechanical transparency, the ability of forces at the output to produce observable motion and current at the motor. The cost is a greater demand on the motor for a given output torque.

Mechanical transparency also changes what motor current can reveal. In a high-friction transmission, current must overcome internal losses as well as the external load. With sufficiently small friction and inertial contributions, the joint torque estimate simplifies to:
$$\tau_{\text{joint}} \approx \eta N K_t I_q$$
Motor current can then support **proprioceptive sensing** of interaction torque. The estimate requires calibration across the operating conditions; current remains a measurement of motor effort, and acceleration or friction can consume part of that effort. Backdrivability allows contact to move the joint, but neither low gearing nor current sensing alone establishes a safe impact force.

[^fn-hist-qdd-lineage]: **Lineage of direct drive and quasi-direct drive (QDD) robotics**: Direct drive manipulation was pioneered by Haruhiko Asada and Takeo Kanade at CMU (1983), eliminating transmission backlash and friction at the expense of heavy, bulky motors. The modern Quasi-Direct Drive (QDD) paradigm was established by Sangbae Kim, Patrick Wensing, and Benjamin Katz at MIT (Cheetah 3 and Mini Cheetah, 2017–2019), demonstrating that low single-stage planetary gear reductions ($N \le 10{:}1$) preserve backdrivability and proprioceptive current sensing while multiplying continuous torque density fourfold.

For a contact-dominated arm, the choice is a joint whose measured compliance, torque response, and sensing support the intended interaction [@seok2015design; @wensing2017proprioceptive]. Load-side position or torque sensing can expose disagreement hidden by the motor encoder, allowing the permission path to reject further force commands when the qualified response no longer holds.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Mechanical gearhead fatigue cycles set the sample efficiency limits for reinforcement learning in @sec-training-learning-by-trial.
:::

### Supporting drive and impedance models {#sec-body-drive-supporting-models}

The actuator decision above depends on measured torque, response time, and contact behavior. For readers inspecting a drive implementation, the following coordinate model explains how FOC represents the torque-producing current. Current sensors measure the three phase currents $(i_a, i_b, i_c)$. Using the amplitude-invariant convention, the Clarke transform projects these currents onto a stationary two-axis frame $(\alpha, \beta)$:
   $$\begin{bmatrix} i_\alpha \\ i_\beta \end{bmatrix} = \frac{2}{3}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -\frac{1}{2} & -\frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} i_a \\ i_b \\ i_c \end{bmatrix}$$

The measured shaft angle $\theta_m$ determines electrical angle $\theta_e = P_n \theta_m$, where $P_n$ is the number of magnetic pole pairs. The Park transform rotates the stationary currents into a frame $(d, q)$ aligned with the rotor flux:
   $$\begin{bmatrix} i_d \\ i_q \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta_e & \sin\theta_e \\ -\sin\theta_e & \cos\theta_e \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} i_\alpha \\ i_\beta \end{bmatrix}$$
In the torque model used here, the controller regulates quadrature current $i_q$ for torque while keeping direct-axis current $i_d$ near zero:
   $$\tau = \frac{3}{2} P_n \Phi_m i_q = K_t i_q$$
Here $\Phi_m$ denotes permanent-magnet flux linkage. Current feedback determines voltage requests; inverse coordinate transforms and pulse-width modulation turn them into inverter switching duty cycles. The current convention used in a drive must match the convention used to identify its torque constant.

For readers using frequency-domain models, mechanical impedance expresses the joint's resistance to imposed motion. With $s$ the Laplace frequency variable, the apparent mechanical impedance $Z_{\text{out}}(s) = \tau_{\text{ext}}(s) / \dot{q}(s)$ at the output flange is:
$$Z_{\text{out}}(s) = s \left(J_{\text{load}} + N^2 J_{\text{rotor}}\right) + B_{\text{joint}} + N^2 B_{\text{motor}} + \frac{K_{\text{joint}}}{s}$$
The coefficients $B_{\text{joint}}$ and $B_{\text{motor}}$ describe viscous damping, and $K_{\text{joint}}$ describes torsional stiffness. The terms collect resistance due to acceleration, velocity, and displacement. Their engineering consequence is the one already used in transmission selection: gearing magnifies rotor inertia and damping, while compliance and friction also determine contact behavior.

Operating near the resulting current and torque limits has a thermodynamic cost. Every ampere that accelerates rotor inertia or sustains peak torque dissipates $I^2 R$ in the copper, and that heat accumulates in the actuator's thermal mass, bounding how long peak torque can last before insulation breaks down.

## Thermal Duty Cycles {#sec-body-thermal-duty-cycles}

Holding a load motionless at full reach places deceptive demands on an articulated arm such as the mobile manipulator's. Maintaining a static load against gravity demands continuous phase current through the stator coils, actively converting electrical energy into accumulating heat. **Heat arrives in seconds and leaves in minutes, making duty cycle a primary design variable.**

### Thermal capacity and insulation breakdown thresholds {#sec-body-thermal-capacity}

In classical mechanics, holding a stationary mass stationary involves zero mechanical work ($W = \int F \cdot dx = 0$). In an electromechanical robot, however, sustaining holding torque against gravity requires continuous phase current to produce magnetic Lorentz force ($\tau = K_t I$). The lumped thermal model uses $I$ in the same convention as its torque constant $K_t$. Here $R$ denotes the effective aggregate loss resistance for that current, so total winding copper loss is:
$$P_{\text{loss}} = I^2 R = \frac{\tau^2}{K_t^2} R$$
For the amplitude-invariant drive convention above, with balanced phase currents, $I=i_q$ and $i_d=0$, this effective resistance is $R=R_{\text{eff}}=\frac{3}{2}R_{\text{phase}}$, where $R_{\text{phase}}$ is resistance per phase. Thus $R$ in the thermal calculations includes the phase-summing factor; it is not the per-phase resistance used in the earlier electrical current-rise model. The following illustrative thermal examples stipulate this effective resistance and matching current convention.

This equation reveals the fundamental physical identity of electric actuation: **torque is current, and current is heat.** Commanded torque scales linearly with current ($\tau = K_t I$), but stator copper loss scales **quadratically with torque** ($\tau^2$). Demanding twice the torque requires four times the thermal dissipation. Because heat has no fast exit, thermal accumulation limits how long an arm can maintain static poses or execute dynamic bursts without mechanical brakes.

Reducing motor current to shed heat also reduces holding torque. A loaded arm therefore needs a response that preserves support, such as transferring the load to a mechanical brake, rather than assuming that thermal derating leaves the task unchanged. Excess winding temperature can damage electrical insulation, while excess rotor temperature can permanently reduce magnet strength. Those material limits bound the allowable temperature trajectory.

The winding and housing respond on different timescales. Copper heats rapidly under current, while the larger core and housing absorb and reject heat more slowly. A case temperature measurement can therefore lag the winding hotspot during a torque burst.

::: {#fig-02-real-burnt-motor-stator fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Stator winding insulation breakdown**: Cutaway view of a damaged electric motor stator showing critical thermal subsystems: (1) copper phase windings (primary $I^2 R$ heat source), (2) dielectric slot liners and Nomex insulation breakdown threshold ($155^\circ\text{C}$, Class F), (3) laminated iron stator core ($C_{\text{th}}$ and dissipation path $\theta_{JA}$), and (4) rotor bore air gap and magnet thermal limits ($80^\circ\text{C}\text{--}150^\circ\text{C}$). (Source: Industrial Electromechanical Diagnostics Archive, CC BY 4.0)." fig-alt="Annotated photograph of a damaged motor stator with callout badges highlighting copper phase windings, dielectric slot liners, laminated stator core, and rotor bore."}
![](images/jpg/fig02_real_burnt_motor_stator_annotated.jpg){width="85%"}
:::

A thermal model follows the same energy accounting as the stopping calculation: energy accumulates where the rate entering exceeds the rate leaving. Here the winding receives electrical losses and transfers heat to the core; the core transfers heat to the surroundings. Thermal capacitance measures how much energy raises a component's temperature, while thermal resistance measures how strongly the heat-flow path resists that transfer. Representing the winding and core separately gives the two-node lumped-parameter thermal ordinary differential equation (ODE) system:
$$\begin{aligned}
C_{\text{wind}} \frac{dT_{\text{wind}}(t)}{dt} &= P_{\text{loss}}(t) - \frac{T_{\text{wind}}(t) - T_{\text{core}}(t)}{R_{\text{th, wc}}} \\
C_{\text{core}} \frac{dT_{\text{core}}(t)}{dt} &= \frac{T_{\text{wind}}(t) - T_{\text{core}}(t)}{R_{\text{th, wc}}} - \frac{T_{\text{core}}(t) - T_{\text{amb}}}{R_{\text{th, ca}}}
\end{aligned}$$
where $P_{\text{loss}}(t) = I^2(t) R(T_{\text{wind}}) = \frac{\tau^2(t)}{K_t^2} R(T_{\text{wind}})$ is the Joule dissipation source deposited directly into the copper coils, $C_{\text{wind}}$ is the small thermal capacitance of the winding, $C_{\text{core}}$ is the large thermal capacitance of the laminated stator core and housing, $R_{\text{th, wc}}$ is the conductive thermal resistance from winding to core, and $R_{\text{th, ca}}$ is the convective thermal resistance from core to ambient air.

This separation of timescales creates a dangerous observability gap. Because $C_{\text{wind}} \ll C_{\text{core}}$, under a sudden peak torque burst or sustained stall against gravity, the stator core temperature $T_{\text{core}}$ remains virtually clamped over the initial seconds by its large thermal inertia. The internal copper winding temperature surges at the initial adiabatic rate:
$$\left.\frac{dT_{\text{wind}}}{dt}\right|_{t=0} \approx \frac{P_{\text{loss}}}{C_{\text{wind}}}$$
Within 15 to 30 seconds of sustained peak torque, the internal copper hotspot $T_{\text{wind}}$ can surge past the $155^\circ\text{C}$ Class F dielectric limit, blistering polyimide slot insulation and triggering turn-to-turn short circuits (@fig-02-real-burnt-motor-stator), even while an external thermistor bonded to the motor casing measures a deceptively benign $45^\circ\text{C}$ to $50^\circ\text{C}$.

A first-order approximation can summarize heating over a characterized operating range, with an effective temperature $T$ and fitted thermal parameters:
$$C_{\text{th}} \frac{dT(t)}{dt} = P_{\text{loss}}(t) - \frac{T(t) - T_{\text{amb}}}{\theta_{JA}}$$
where $\theta_{JA} = R_{\text{th, wc}} + R_{\text{th, ca}}$ represents the winding-to-ambient steady-state thermal resistance. The effective capacitance $C_{\text{th}}$ sets the fitted time constant $\tau_{\text{th}} = \theta_{JA} C_{\text{th}}$. This approximation does not resolve a fast winding hotspot separately from the housing; its transient predictions require validation before they can bound a burst.

At thermal steady state ($dT/dt = 0$), heat generation balances heat dissipation to ambient:
$$P_{\text{loss, ss}} = \frac{T_{\max} - T_{\text{amb}}}{\theta_{JA}}$$
Substituting the copper loss identity $P_{\text{loss}} = \frac{\tau^2}{K_t^2} R(T_{\max})$ reveals the **continuous thermal torque ceiling**:
$$\tau_{\text{cont}} = K_t \sqrt{\frac{T_{\max} - T_{\text{amb}}}{R(T_{\max}) \theta_{JA}}}$$
**Continuous torque is limited by thermal dissipation ($T_{\max} \approx 150^\circ\text{C}$), not peak silicon or battery current ratings.** An actuator rated for $30\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ peak acceleration torque may sustain only $8\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ continuously. A brief torque burst of several seconds causes a rapid transient temperature rise that remains safe if peak temperature stays below insulation ratings ($T_{\text{limit}} = 155^\circ\text{C}$). However, sustained holding torque or high-frequency cycling drives the winding toward an asymptotic thermal equilibrium $T_\infty = T_{\text{amb}} + \bar{P}_{\text{loss}} \theta_{JA}$. If that equilibrium exceeds the insulation threshold, continuous operation destroys the stator winding enamel and causes phase-to-phase short circuits.

```{python}
#| label: body-copper-resistance-rise-calc
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ COPPER RESISTANCE RISE TO THE ENGINEERING CEILING (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: the simulation-policy paragraph in @sec-body-thermal-duty-cycles.
# │ Goal:    Price copper's temperature coefficient between the resistance
# │          reference and the engineering ceiling of the thermal notebooks.
# │ Show:    alpha_Cu = 0.00393 1/K; 20 C to 140 C raises R by 47.2 percent,
# │          and I^2 R at fixed current by the same fraction.
# │ How:     R(T)/R_0 - 1 = alpha_Cu (T - T_0).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_math, fmt_temperature, fmt_percent, check

K = ureg.kelvin

class CopperResistanceRise:
    """Fractional rise of winding resistance from 20 C to the 140 C engineering ceiling."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    alpha_cu = 0.00393 / K  # category: sourced (annealed copper, 100 percent IACS, at 20 C; NBS Handbook 100, Copper Wire Tables)
    t_0 = ureg.Quantity(20.0, ureg.degC).to(K)  # category: illustrative (resistance reference)
    t_ceiling = ureg.Quantity(140.0, ureg.degC).to(K)  # category: chosen (engineering ceiling)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    rise = (alpha_cu * (t_ceiling - t_0)).to("dimensionless").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(rise - 0.4716) < 1e-4, f"Resistance rise must be 47.2 percent: {rise}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    alpha_cu_math = fmt_math(rf"\alpha_{{\text{{Cu}}}} \approx {fmt(alpha_cu.magnitude, precision=5, commas=False)}\text{{ K}}^{{-1}}")
    t_0_str = fmt_temperature(t_0, unit=ureg.degC, precision=0)
    t_ceiling_str = fmt_temperature(t_ceiling, unit=ureg.degC, precision=0)
    rise_pct_str = fmt_percent(rise, precision=1, style="prose")
```

The loss term must also change with temperature. Copper's positive temperature coefficient\index{Copper resistance!temperature dependence}\index{Stator resistance!thermal coefficient} (`{python} CopperResistanceRise.alpha_cu_math`) increases the effective winding resistance by `{python} CopperResistanceRise.rise_pct_str` from `{python} CopperResistanceRise.t_0_str` to the `{python} CopperResistanceRise.t_ceiling_str` engineering ceiling, according to $R(T) = R_0 [1 + \alpha_{\text{Cu}}(T - T_0)]$. Holding the same torque therefore dissipates `{python} CopperResistanceRise.rise_pct_str` more winding power. A fixed-resistance calculation omits this feedback; the burst example below uses that approximation explicitly, and the subsequent stall calculation restores it.

Datasheet thermal ratings are optimistic because they are measured on an unconstrained motor mounted to a large heat sink in free air at $20^\circ\text{C}$ or $25^\circ\text{C}$. Installed in a sealed chassis beside power electronics, battery packs, and other joints, the motor loses convective airflow, which raises $\theta_{JA}$, and neighboring loads can raise its local ambient to $45^\circ\text{C}$ to $55^\circ\text{C}$ before its own coils carry current. Thermal margins must therefore be budgeted from heating and cooling time constants measured with the enclosure sealed and adjacent loads at their $P_{99}$ power draw.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Real-time telemetry for thermal and power integrity budgets is transported by the deterministic fieldbuses analyzed in @sec-nervous-deterministic-fieldbuses.
:::

### Transient thermal bursts and periodic duty cycles {#sec-body-transient-thermal-bursts}

Because thermal capacity integrates power over time, a peak torque[^fn-hw-motor-intermittent] or peak current rating is meaningless without four parameters: the initial winding temperature $T(0)$, the allowed duration $t_{\text{on}}$, the ambient $T_{\text{amb}}$, and the recovery time $t_{\text{off}}$. An actuator that can produce three times its continuous torque sustains it only while the integral of $I^2 R$ stays within the margin below the insulation limit, which from a cold winding can last tens of seconds and from a heat-soaked one a fraction of that (\ref{nbk-body-thermal-burst-limits}).

[^fn-hw-motor-intermittent]: **Actuator Intermittent Duty Limits**\index{Actuator!intermittent torque}: Robotics motor datasheets prominently advertise peak torque ($\tau_{\text{peak}}$), but this rating is strictly intermittent, and how long it can be held depends on the winding's starting temperature. Sustained dynamic maneuvering must be budgeted against continuous root-mean-square torque ($\tau_{\text{cont}}$), otherwise aggressive neural policy commands will trip thermal protection and cause mid-motion limb collapse.

```{python}
#| label: body-thermal-burst-calc
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THERMAL BURST HORIZONS AND THE DUTY-CYCLE SCREEN (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: \ref{nbk-body-thermal-burst-limits}, the duty-cycle paragraph in
# │          @sec-body-thermal-duty-cycles, and the ranking of margins in
# │          @sec-body-archetype-matrix.
# │ Goal:    Price a threefold current burst in an arm shoulder joint from a
# │          cold and a heat-soaked start, then test the average-power duty
# │          screen against the first-order periodic peak.
# │ Show:    cold 56.0 s, hot 20.7 s (63.1 percent less); duty <= 14.8 percent;
# │          3 s on, 17.3 s off; the periodic peak reaches 142.7 C > 140 C.
# │ How:     First-order lumped model, fixed R: T(t) = T_inf - (T_inf - T0)
# │          exp(-t/tau); periodic peak rise P theta (1 - e^-ton/tau) /
# │          (1 - e^-tcycle/tau), with the screened off-time rounded up to 0.1 s.
# │ Note:    Reads t_ceiling from CopperResistanceRise (earlier cell) so the
# │          140 C engineering ceiling is declared once.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import (
    fmt,
    fmt_heat_capacity,
    fmt_thermal_resistance,
    fmt_latency,
    fmt_power,
    fmt_current,
    fmt_resistance,
    fmt_temperature,
    fmt_percent,
    check,
)

K = ureg.kelvin

class ThermalBurst:
    """Burst horizons, duty-cycle screen, and periodic peak for an arm shoulder joint."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    r_wind = 1.2 * ureg.ohm  # category: illustrative (aggregate loss resistance for amplitude-invariant i_q, i_d=0; held fixed)
    c_th = 120.0 * joule / K  # category: illustrative (lumped thermal capacitance)
    theta_ja = 2.5 * K / ureg.watt  # category: illustrative (installed thermal resistance)
    t_amb = ureg.Quantity(40.0, ureg.degC).to(K)  # category: illustrative (enclosed ambient)
    t_limit = ureg.Quantity(155.0, ureg.degC).to(K)  # category: sourced (IEC 60085 Class F hotspot)
    t_ceiling = CopperResistanceRise.t_ceiling  # category: chosen (engineering ceiling, declared once in CopperResistanceRise)
    i_cont = 5.0 * ureg.ampere  # category: illustrative (continuous amplitude-invariant i_q, i_d=0)
    i_peak = 15.0 * ureg.ampere  # category: illustrative (threefold i_q burst)
    t_on = 3.0 * second  # category: illustrative (burst length)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    tau = (theta_ja * c_th).to(second)
    p_cont = (i_cont**2 * r_wind).to(ureg.watt)
    t_equil = (t_amb + p_cont * theta_ja).to(K)
    p_peak = (i_peak**2 * r_wind).to(ureg.watt)
    t_inf = (t_amb + p_peak * theta_ja).to(K)
    t_cold = (tau * math.log(((t_inf - t_amb) / (t_inf - t_limit)).to("dimensionless").magnitude)).to(second)
    t_hot = (tau * math.log(((t_inf - t_equil) / (t_inf - t_limit)).to("dimensionless").magnitude)).to(second)
    hot_cut = (1 - t_hot / t_cold).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    p_avg_max = ((t_ceiling - t_amb) / theta_ja).to(ureg.watt)
    duty = (p_avg_max / p_peak).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    t_off = (t_on * (1 - duty) / duty).to(second)
    t_off_sched = math.ceil(t_off.magnitude * 10) / 10 * second  # screening value rounded up to 0.1 s
    t_cycle = t_on + t_off_sched
    rise_peak = (
        p_peak
        * theta_ja
        * (1 - math.exp(-(t_on / tau).to("dimensionless").magnitude))
        / (1 - math.exp(-(t_cycle / tau).to("dimensionless").magnitude))
    )
    t_peak = (t_amb + rise_peak).to(K)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(tau.magnitude - 300.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected time constant: {tau}")
    check(abs(p_cont.magnitude - 30.0) < 1e-9 and abs(p_peak.magnitude - 270.0) < 1e-9, "Unexpected dissipation.")
    check(abs(t_equil.to(ureg.degC).magnitude - 115.0) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected equilibrium: {t_equil}")
    check(abs(t_inf.to(ureg.degC).magnitude - 715.0) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected asymptote: {t_inf}")
    check(abs(t_cold.magnitude - 56.03) < 0.01, f"Cold-start horizon must be 56.0 s: {t_cold}")
    check(abs(t_hot.magnitude - 20.70) < 0.01, f"Hot-start horizon must be 20.7 s: {t_hot}")
    check(abs(duty - 40.0 / 270.0) < 1e-12, f"Unexpected duty cycle: {duty}")
    check(abs(t_off_sched.magnitude - 17.3) < 1e-9, f"Screening off-time must be 17.3 s: {t_off_sched}")
    check(t_peak > t_ceiling, "The screened schedule must overshoot the 140 C ceiling.")
    check(abs(t_peak.to(ureg.degC).magnitude - 142.65) < 0.01, f"Periodic peak must be about 142.65 C: {t_peak}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    r_wind_str = fmt_resistance(r_wind, unit=ureg.ohm, precision=1)
    c_th_str = fmt_heat_capacity(c_th, unit=joule / K, precision=0)
    theta_ja_str = fmt_thermal_resistance(theta_ja, precision=1)
    t_amb_str = fmt_temperature(t_amb, unit=ureg.degC, precision=0)
    t_limit_str = fmt_temperature(t_limit, unit=ureg.degC, precision=0)
    t_ceiling_str = fmt_temperature(t_ceiling, unit=ureg.degC, precision=0)
    tau_str = fmt_latency(tau, unit=second, precision=0)
    i_cont_str = fmt_current(i_cont, unit=ureg.ampere, precision=0)
    i_peak_str = fmt_current(i_peak, unit=ureg.ampere, precision=0)
    p_peak_str = fmt_power(p_peak, unit=ureg.watt, precision=0)
    p_avg_max_str = fmt_power(p_avg_max, unit=ureg.watt, precision=0)
    t_equil_str = fmt_temperature(t_equil, unit=ureg.degC, precision=0)
    t_inf_str = fmt_temperature(t_inf, unit=ureg.degC, precision=0)
    t_cold_str = fmt_latency(t_cold, unit=second, precision=1)
    t_hot_str = fmt_latency(t_hot, unit=second, precision=1)
    hot_cut_pct_str = fmt_percent(hot_cut, precision=1, style="prose")
    duty_pct_str = fmt_percent(duty, precision=1, style="prose")
    t_on_str = fmt_latency(t_on, unit=second, precision=0)
    t_off_str = fmt_latency(t_off_sched, unit=second, precision=1)
    t_peak_str = fmt_temperature(t_peak, unit=ureg.degC, precision=1)
```

::: {#nbk-body-thermal-burst-limits .callout-notebook title="Thermal accumulation across duty cycles"}
An illustrative arm shoulder joint has effective aggregate loss resistance $R =$ `{python} ThermalBurst.r_wind_str`, lumped thermal capacitance $C_{\text{th}} =$ `{python} ThermalBurst.c_th_str`, and installed thermal resistance $\theta_{JA} =$ `{python} ThermalBurst.theta_ja_str`, and it runs in an enclosed ambient $T_{\text{amb}} =$ `{python} ThermalBurst.t_amb_str` with Class F insulation rated to `{python} ThermalBurst.t_limit_str`. The thermal time constant is $\tau = \theta_{JA} C_{\text{th}} =$ `{python} ThermalBurst.tau_str`.

**Problem**: How does the initial winding temperature change how long a threefold rated-current burst can last before the insulation limit?

**Math**:

1. **Continuous equilibrium**: At $I_{\text{cont}} =$ `{python} ThermalBurst.i_cont_str` the winding settles at $T_{\text{eq}} = T_{\text{amb}} + I_{\text{cont}}^2 R\,\theta_{JA} =$ `{python} ThermalBurst.t_equil_str`, below the limit.
2. **Peak burst**: At $I_{\text{peak}} =$ `{python} ThermalBurst.i_peak_str` the dissipation rises ninefold to $P_{\text{peak}} =$ `{python} ThermalBurst.p_peak_str`, whose asymptote $T_\infty = T_{\text{amb}} + P_{\text{peak}}\theta_{JA} =$ `{python} ThermalBurst.t_inf_str` lies far above the limit.
3. **Survival horizons**: With $T(t) = T_\infty - (T_\infty - T(0))\,e^{-t/\tau}$, the time to reach the limit is
   $$t_{\text{limit}} = \tau \ln\frac{T_\infty - T(0)}{T_\infty - T_{\text{limit}}}$$
   which gives `{python} ThermalBurst.t_cold_str` from a cold start at ambient and `{python} ThermalBurst.t_hot_str` from a heat-soaked start at $T_{\text{eq}}$.

**Result**: The heat-soaked joint holds the burst `{python} ThermalBurst.hot_cut_pct_str` less time than the cold one, so peak torque cannot be budgeted without tracking thermal history.
:::

For repeated cycles of period $t_{\text{cycle}} = t_{\text{on}} + t_{\text{off}}$, an engineering ceiling $T_{\max} =$ `{python} ThermalBurst.t_ceiling_str` sets a cycle-average power ceiling $\bar{P}_{\max} = (T_{\max} - T_{\text{amb}})/\theta_{JA} =$ `{python} ThermalBurst.p_avg_max_str`. With peak dissipation during $t_{\text{on}}$ and none during $t_{\text{off}}$, this average-power screen bounds the duty cycle $D = t_{\text{on}}/t_{\text{cycle}}$ by
$$D \le \frac{T_{\max} - T_{\text{amb}}}{P_{\text{peak}} \theta_{JA}}$$
which here is `{python} ThermalBurst.duty_pct_str`, so a `{python} ThermalBurst.t_on_str` burst calls for a recovery of $t_{\text{off}} = t_{\text{on}}(1 - D)/D \approx$ `{python} ThermalBurst.t_off_str`. The average does not bound the hottest instant: because heat arrives in seconds during bursts but dissipates over minutes during recovery, the peak transient hotspot temperature during periodic pulsing strictly exceeds the time-averaged calculation,[^fn-math-thermal-peak] reaching `{python} ThermalBurst.t_peak_str` (above the ceiling) before the rise of $R(T)$ adds more. Average-power screening is optimistic, and a burst schedule is certified only against the transient hotspot trajectory.

[^fn-math-thermal-peak]: **Periodic steady-state thermal peak derivation**: In a periodic duty cycle of period $t_{\text{cycle}} = t_{\text{on}} + t_{\text{off}}$, summing the geometric series of heating and cooling exponentials yields the exact periodic peak temperature rise: $\Delta T_{\text{peak}} = P_{\text{peak}}\theta_{JA}\frac{1 - e^{-t_{\text{on}}/\tau}}{1 - e^{-t_{\text{cycle}}/\tau}}$. As $t_{\text{cycle}} \to 0$, this converges to the average-power screen ($D P_{\text{peak}}\theta_{JA}$); for finite burst durations, peak winding temperature strictly exceeds the average.

### Torque-speed operating envelopes and back-EMF roll-off {#sec-body-torque-speed-envelopes}

The burst calculation limits duration, while the back-EMF relation in @sec-body-electrical-time-constants limits torque at speed. A feasible maneuver must satisfy both. At low speed, the drive can supply the current needed for a burst, but the winding temperature limits how long it may do so. At higher speed, back-EMF consumes voltage headroom and can prevent that current from appearing at all. The torque-speed envelope in @fig-02-motor-torque-speed-envelope combines these constraints instead of treating peak torque as available at every speed and duration.

::: {#fig-02-motor-torque-speed-envelope fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Motor torque-speed operating region**: The permanent magnet synchronous motor torque-speed plane, separating continuous duty $S_1$ at thermal equilibrium from intermittent periodic duty $S_3$ at peak acceleration, alongside the exponential thermal accumulation trajectory during peak bursts and conductive cooling during recovery. Winding thermal limits constrain sustainable duty cycle rather than peak inverter current." fig-alt="Torque-speed characteristic curve for a permanent magnet synchronous motor, contrasting the continuous thermal rating zone with the intermittent peak acceleration region, with an adjacent graph showing temperature rise during active bursts and cooling decay."}
![](images/svg/fig02_motor_torque_speed_envelope.svg){width="100%"}
:::

The continuous-duty region ($S_1$) permits sustained operation under the declared cooling conditions. The larger intermittent region ($S_3$) permits periodic bursts only with the starting temperature, duration, and recovery interval established above. Both regions narrow when speed consumes the drive's voltage headroom. Their intersection with the current thermal state, rather than the catalog peak, gives the available torque for the next maneuver.

A simulator that uses only a fixed torque clamp can therefore teach a policy an unavailable action: maximum torque while the rotor is already near its voltage-limited speed, or a repeated burst without recovery. The actuator model and permission limits must include speed and thermal history. Temperature-dependent winding resistance further shrinks the available region during a sustained hold.

### Copper resistance feedback and stall thermal runaway {#sec-body-copper-resistance-feedback}

The copper-resistance rise calculated in @sec-body-thermal-capacity must enter the runtime estimate as well as the design calculation. An external thermistor can lag the winding hotspot, so a thermal observer combines measured current with the characterized heating and cooling model. A discrete update of the lumped energy balance is:
$$\hat{T}_{k+1} = \hat{T}_k + \frac{\Delta t}{C_{\text{th}}} \left[ I_k^2 R(\hat{T}_k) - \frac{\hat{T}_k - T_{\text{amb}}}{\theta_{JA}} \right]$$
where $R(\hat{T}_k) = R_0 [1 + \alpha_{\text{Cu}}(\hat{T}_k - T_0)]$. The update interval, model error, and temperature uncertainty must fit the thermal margin. As the estimate approaches its ceiling, the permission path reduces admissible effort or transfers the load to a qualified support mechanism. Removing holding current without securing a gravity-loaded arm would exchange a thermal fault for uncontrolled motion. A static hold shows how copper's feedback changes the sustainable torque (\ref{nbk-body-thermal-stall-derating}).

```{python}
#| label: body-thermal-stall-calc
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ STALL RUNAWAY AND THERMAL DERATING (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: \ref{nbk-body-thermal-stall-derating} in @sec-body-thermal-duty-cycles.
# │ Goal:    Find where a stalled arm elbow's winding settles once copper's
# │          resistance rises with temperature, and the hold it can sustain.
# │ Show:    10 A stall, 80 W cold; steady rise 357.8 K (397.8 C); sustainable
# │          63.89 W at 1.224 Ohm hot, 7.22 A, 30.7 N m (27.8 percent derating).
# │ How:     Steady state dT = I^2 R0 [1 + alpha (T_amb - T0 + dT)] theta solved
# │          for dT; derating from P_max = (T_limit - T_amb)/theta at R(T_limit).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import (
    fmt,
    fmt_int,
    fmt_torque,
    fmt_torque_constant,
    fmt_current,
    fmt_resistance,
    fmt_thermal_resistance,
    fmt_power,
    fmt_temperature,
    fmt_percent,
    check,
)

K = ureg.kelvin

class StallDerating:
    """Steady stall temperature under copper's resistance feedback, and the sustainable hold."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    tau_hold = 42.5 * ureg.newton * meter  # category: illustrative (static holding torque)
    k_t = 0.10 * ureg.newton * meter / ureg.ampere  # category: illustrative (torque per amplitude-invariant i_q, i_d=0)
    r_0 = 0.80 * ureg.ohm  # category: illustrative (aggregate loss resistance for i_q at T_0, not per-phase resistance)
    t_0 = ureg.Quantity(20.0, ureg.degC).to(K)  # category: illustrative (resistance reference)
    theta_ja = 1.80 * K / ureg.watt  # category: illustrative (unventilated limb)
    t_amb = ureg.Quantity(40.0, ureg.degC).to(K)  # category: illustrative (limb ambient)
    t_limit = ureg.Quantity(155.0, ureg.degC).to(K)  # category: sourced (IEC 60085 Class F hotspot)
    n_gear = 50  # category: illustrative (cycloidal reduction)
    eta = 0.85  # category: illustrative (gear efficiency)
    alpha_cu = 0.00393 / K  # category: sourced (annealed copper, 100 percent IACS, at 20 C; NBS Handbook 100, Copper Wire Tables)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    tau_motor = (tau_hold / (eta * n_gear)).to(ureg.newton * meter)
    i_stall = (tau_motor / k_t).to(ureg.ampere)
    p_cold = (i_stall**2 * r_0).to(ureg.watt)
    gain = (i_stall**2 * r_0 * theta_ja).to(K)  # rise per unit of resistance factor
    const = (gain * (1 + alpha_cu * (t_amb - t_0))).to(K)
    slope = (gain * alpha_cu).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    dt_ss = (const / (1 - slope)).to(K)
    t_wind = (t_amb + dt_ss).to(K)
    p_max = ((t_limit - t_amb) / theta_ja).to(ureg.watt)
    r_hot = (r_0 * (1 + alpha_cu * (t_limit - t_0))).to(ureg.ohm)
    i_max = ((p_max / r_hot) ** 0.5).to(ureg.ampere)
    tau_hold_max = (eta * n_gear * k_t * i_max).to(ureg.newton * meter)
    derate = (1 - tau_hold_max / tau_hold).to("dimensionless").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(tau_motor.magnitude - 1.0) < 1e-9 and abs(i_stall.magnitude - 10.0) < 1e-9, "Unexpected stall current.")
    check(abs(p_cold.magnitude - 80.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected cold dissipation: {p_cold}")
    check(abs(const.magnitude - 155.32) < 0.01 and abs(slope - 0.5659) < 1e-4, "Unexpected feedback terms.")
    check(abs(dt_ss.magnitude - 357.8) < 0.1, f"Steady rise must be 357.8 K: {dt_ss}")
    check(t_wind > t_limit, "The uncontrolled stall must exceed the insulation limit.")
    check(abs(p_max.magnitude - 63.89) < 0.01, f"Unexpected sustainable dissipation: {p_max}")
    check(abs(i_max.magnitude - 7.22) < 0.01, f"Unexpected sustainable current: {i_max}")
    check(abs(tau_hold_max.magnitude - 30.7) < 0.05, f"Sustainable hold must be 30.7 N m: {tau_hold_max}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    tau_hold_str = fmt_torque(tau_hold, precision=1)
    n_gear_str = fmt_int(n_gear)
    eta_str = fmt(eta, precision=2)
    k_t_str = fmt_torque_constant(k_t, precision=2)
    r_0_str = fmt_resistance(r_0, unit=ureg.ohm, precision=2)
    t_0_str = fmt_temperature(t_0, unit=ureg.degC, precision=0)
    theta_ja_str = fmt_thermal_resistance(theta_ja, precision=2)
    t_amb_str = fmt_temperature(t_amb, unit=ureg.degC, precision=0)
    t_limit_str = fmt_temperature(t_limit, unit=ureg.degC, precision=0)
    tau_motor_str = fmt_torque(tau_motor, precision=0)
    i_stall_str = fmt_current(i_stall, unit=ureg.ampere, precision=0)
    p_cold_str = fmt_power(p_cold, unit=ureg.watt, precision=0)
    const_str = fmt(const.magnitude, precision=2)
    slope_str = fmt(slope, precision=4)
    dt_ss_str = fmt_temperature(dt_ss, unit=ureg.kelvin, precision=1)
    t_wind_str = fmt_temperature(t_wind, unit=ureg.degC, precision=1)
    dt_max_str = fmt_temperature((t_limit - t_amb).to(K), unit=ureg.kelvin, precision=0)
    p_max_str = fmt_power(p_max, unit=ureg.watt, precision=2)
    r_hot_str = fmt_resistance(r_hot, unit=ureg.ohm, precision=3)
    i_max_str = fmt_current(i_max, unit=ureg.ampere, precision=2)
    tau_hold_max_str = fmt_torque(tau_hold_max, precision=1)
    derate_pct_str = fmt_percent(derate, precision=1, style="prose")
```

::: {#nbk-body-thermal-stall-derating .callout-notebook title="Static holding torque and stall derating"}
An arm elbow holds $\tau_{\text{hold}} =$ `{python} StallDerating.tau_hold_str` at stall ($\omega = 0$) through an $N =$ `{python} StallDerating.n_gear_str`:1 cycloidal gearbox ($\eta =$ `{python} StallDerating.eta_str`). Its motor has $K_t =$ `{python} StallDerating.k_t_str`, cold effective aggregate loss resistance $R_0 =$ `{python} StallDerating.r_0_str` at $T_0 =$ `{python} StallDerating.t_0_str`, and $\theta_{JA} =$ `{python} StallDerating.theta_ja_str`, with a Class F limit of `{python} StallDerating.t_limit_str`, inside an unventilated limb at $T_{\text{amb}} =$ `{python} StallDerating.t_amb_str`.

**Problem**: With copper's resistance rising with temperature, where does the stalled winding settle, and what holding torque is thermally sustainable?

**Math**:

1. **Stall current**: $\tau_{\text{motor}} = \tau_{\text{hold}}/(\eta N) =$ `{python} StallDerating.tau_motor_str`, so $I = \tau_{\text{motor}}/K_t =$ `{python} StallDerating.i_stall_str` and the cold dissipation is $P_0 = I^2 R_0 =$ `{python} StallDerating.p_cold_str`.
2. **Runaway**: With $R(T) = R_0[1 + \alpha_{\text{Cu}}(T - T_0)]$, the steady rise satisfies
   $$\Delta T = I^2 R_0 \left[1 + \alpha_{\text{Cu}}(T_{\text{amb}} - T_0 + \Delta T)\right] \theta_{JA}$$
   Rearranging terms yields $\Delta T = \frac{I^2 R_0 [1 + \alpha_{\text{Cu}}(T_{\text{amb}} - T_0)] \theta_{JA}}{1 - I^2 R_0 \theta_{JA} \alpha_{\text{Cu}}}$. The denominator establishes the **thermal runaway criterion**: if the positive feedback loop gain satisfies $I^2 R_0 \theta_{JA} \alpha_{\text{Cu}} \ge 1$, this fixed-current, linear-resistance model cannot settle to a stable thermal equilibrium. Above one, heat generation increases with temperature faster than heat removal, producing exponential growth; at exactly one, the temperature-dependent terms cancel and the remaining positive heating causes linear growth. In this stall scenario, the feedback factor is `{python} StallDerating.slope_str` $< 1$, so temperature settles at a finite (yet fatal) equilibrium: $\Delta T =$ `{python} StallDerating.const_str` $+$ `{python} StallDerating.slope_str` $\Delta T$, yielding $\Delta T =$ `{python} StallDerating.dt_ss_str` and driving the winding to `{python} StallDerating.t_wind_str`, far above its rating.

3. **Derating**: At the limit the allowable rise is `{python} StallDerating.dt_max_str`, so the sustainable dissipation is $P_{\max} = \Delta T_{\max}/\theta_{JA} =$ `{python} StallDerating.p_max_str`. At the hot resistance $R(T_{\text{limit}}) \approx$ `{python} StallDerating.r_hot_str`, that allows $I_{\max} = \sqrt{P_{\max}/R} \approx$ `{python} StallDerating.i_max_str` and a hold of $\tau_{\text{hold,max}} = \eta N K_t I_{\max} \approx$ `{python} StallDerating.tau_hold_max_str`.

**Result**: Held without control, the stall drives the winding toward `{python} StallDerating.t_wind_str`, and staying within the insulation rating requires a `{python} StallDerating.derate_pct_str` derating, from `{python} StallDerating.tau_hold_str` to `{python} StallDerating.tau_hold_max_str`. Continuous gravity holding above the qualified continuous torque requires another support mechanism, such as a friction brake or counterweight; holding within that torque can remain electrically sustained under the stated thermal conditions.
:::

Delivering the current pulses that generate these thermal loads also stresses the upstream electrical supply, moving the burden from heat in the copper to transient current on the power bus.

## Electrical Power Integrity {#sec-body-power-integrity}

When the mobile manipulator swerves hard to avoid a collision, every drive motor, joint inverter, and accelerator demands peak current at once from one direct-current distribution bus. In simulation, current flows from an idealized source. On hardware, delivery is bounded by finite capacity, source impedance, and transient voltage stability. **A machine that browns out mid-motion fails physically; the electrical supply is a shared resource.**

Rail sag, regenerative overvoltage, and thermal accumulation are manifestations of one bounded energy network on different time scales. Of the three, voltage moves fastest, within microseconds to milliseconds whenever current demand exceeds what the source can deliver at that instant. Compute, sensing, and motor inverters draw from a common bus, so when a policy commands coordinated accelerations across several joints, the sum of their currents changes the voltage delivered to every node on the machine.

### Power distribution impedance, transient droop, and brownout resets {#sec-body-power-distribution-impedance}

The mobile machine's battery, harnesses, connectors, and protection switches all contribute source impedance.[^fn-hw-bus-resistance] Local capacitors supply part of a sudden load increase, so current drawn by the loads need not equal current arriving through the harness. For a source feeding one bus node through resistance and inductance,
$$V_{\text{source}}(t)-V_{\text{bus}}(t)=R_{\text{bus}}I_{\text{source}}(t)+L_{\text{bus}}\frac{dI_{\text{source}}}{dt}$$ {#eq-body-droop}
where $R_{\text{bus}}$ is the lumped source resistance, $L_{\text{bus}}$ is the loop inductance, and $I_{\text{source}}$ is the current through that source path. The local capacitor bank $C_{\text{bus}}$ supplies the difference between load current $I_{\text{load}}$ and source current. In the ideal-capacitor model, charge removed from that bank lowers the same bus voltage:
$$V_{\text{bus}}(0)-V_{\text{bus}}(t)=\frac{1}{C_{\text{bus}}}\int_0^t\left[I_{\text{load}}(s)-I_{\text{source}}(s)\right]ds.$$
These equations jointly determine the voltage response; the capacitor's voltage change is not an additional drop to add to @eq-body-droop. @Sec-appendix-systems-power develops this source-and-capacitor model.

Compute and motion must be budgeted together because they share this path. An obstacle response can require fresh inference at the same time as a large drive-current change. Testing each load separately misses the combined step that the supply must support.

Harness inductance limits how quickly source current can rise. Local capacitors supply the initial current deficit, while harness resistance continues to lower the rail after source current catches up with a sustained load. Once the currents settle, the inductive voltage is zero and the sustained drop is $I_{\text{source}}R_{\text{bus}}$. The worked example below screens that sustained condition; it does not establish the minimum voltage during the transient. If the actual voltage crosses a regulator's undervoltage threshold, computation or communication may stop or reset. Power qualification must establish the voltage at the supplied devices during coincident load and the physical response if those devices lose power.

[^fn-hw-bus-resistance]: **Power distribution bus impedance and capacitor buffering**\index{Bus impedance!power distribution}\index{Brownout reset!undervoltage}: The lumped source resistance is $R_{\text{bus}} = R_{\text{cell}} + R_{\text{harness}} + R_{\text{switch}}$, the sum of battery cell, harness and connector, and protection-switch on-state resistances. Source inductance governs how quickly harness current changes; capacitor discharge bridges the resulting current deficit. Both affect the same bus voltage, so their effects must be solved together rather than added as independent droop estimates. Capacitor series resistance and the actual source response also matter during a transient. The sustained ohmic sag alone is enough to reject the depleted-battery case below.

That reset turns the electrical fault into a mechanical one. Voltage supervisors pull the reset line on microcontrollers and gate drivers, clocks halt, register configurations vanish, and communication buses float. An acceleration command issued just before the reset stays physically active until the gate-driver stage collapses. If the driver then floats, phase current ceases, torque falls to zero, and the body coasts under gravity and inertia into workpieces or hardstops. If it instead shorts the low-side switches for dynamic braking, back-EMF ($e_{\text{bemf}} = K_e \omega$) produces an immediate, violent counter-torque that jerks the mechanics at the joint limits.

```{python}
#| label: body-spring-brake-calc
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ SPRING-BRAKE ENGAGEMENT ON THE RUNNING MACHINE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: the unpowered-states paragraph in @sec-body-power-integrity.
# │ Goal:    Give the interval after coil decay during which a spring-applied
# │          brake on any of the machine's nine axes has not yet engaged.
# │ Show:    30 ms to 80 ms.
# │ How:     RM.spring_brake_engage_min and RM.spring_brake_engage_max.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class SpringBrake:
    """Spring-brake engagement window after coil decay."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    t_engage_min = RM.spring_brake_engage_min  # category: illustrative (fast end)
    t_engage_max = RM.spring_brake_engage_max  # category: illustrative (slow end)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_window = (t_engage_max - t_engage_min).to(millisecond)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(t_engage_min.to(millisecond).magnitude - 30.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected fast engage: {t_engage_min}")
    check(abs(t_engage_max.to(millisecond).magnitude - 80.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected slow engage: {t_engage_max}")
    check(t_window.magnitude > 0, "The slow end must follow the fast end.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    t_engage_min_str = fmt_latency(t_engage_min, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_engage_max_str = fmt_latency(t_engage_max, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
```

### Unpowered states and unmanaged fallback dynamics {#sec-body-unpowered-states}

Power removal is an unmanaged state transition, not an automatic return to safety. Cutting power leaves an actuator in one of three unpowered states, namely free coasting, phase-short dynamic braking, or spring-engaged mechanical braking, and each enforces a distinct mechanical behavior. An electromechanical friction brake requires `{python} SpringBrake.t_engage_min_str` to `{python} SpringBrake.t_engage_max_str` for its mechanical spring to overcome magnetic coil decay and engage its friction pads, during which gravity accelerates an overhead arm downward. Phase-short dynamic braking generates counter-torque directly proportional to angular velocity ($\tau = \frac{K_t K_e}{R_{\text{phase}}} \omega$), providing electromechanical damping at speed but generating zero holding torque at zero velocity. Free coasting simply allows gravity to accelerate unconstrained joints without any resistance. The trajectory a machine follows after an electrical cutoff must be measured under full mechanical payload, not deduced from circuit diagrams. The choice of which safe fallback state the machine should enter belongs to system safety architecture in @sec-enforcement, but the physical dynamics of an unpowered joint are unalterable mechanical constraints of the body.

### Regenerative overvoltage surges and dynamic brake choppers {#sec-body-regenerative-surges}

Regenerative deceleration drives the bus toward its opposite boundary, overvoltage, as part of the machine's kinetic energy returns electrically. **Returned braking energy needs an absorption or dissipation path.** A battery cannot be assumed to accept it under every state of charge, temperature, or protection state. If the battery management system disconnects charge input, the remaining bus components must handle the regenerated energy without exceeding their voltage ratings.

Under the conservative assumption that the battery management system has disconnected and the local bus capacitance $C_{\text{bus}}$ must absorb the entire returned kinetic energy $E_{\text{regen}}$ without dissipation, the terminal DC bus voltage rises to:
$$V_{\text{final}} = \sqrt{V_{\text{initial}}^2 + \frac{2 E_{\text{regen}}}{C_{\text{bus}}}}$$
where $V_{\text{initial}}$ is the nominal rail voltage prior to deceleration (@sec-appendix-systems derives this energy balance).

The capacitor-only endpoint is a screening calculation: if it exceeds a component rating, the stop requires another energy path. A dynamic brake chopper switches an absorption resistor across the bus when voltage reaches a chosen clamp threshold.[^fn-hw-brake-chopper] Its resistor must handle both the peak regenerated power and the pulse energy, with enough recovery between stops. The worked bus calculation below sizes the peak-power requirement for the warehouse machine.

[^fn-hw-brake-chopper]: **Dynamic Braking Chopper Circuit**\index{Dynamic brake chopper!regenerative clamp}\index{Overvoltage protection!dynamic braking}: A power switch and a low-inductance braking resistor placed across the DC bus. When regenerated energy drives the bus above a comparator threshold, the switch conducts and the resistor dissipates the excess as heat, clamping the bus below the breakdown rating of the inverter and converter silicon.

Power integrity is an architectural constraint. The design sets coordinated power budgets and current slew-rate limits across accelerators and drives, the permission path arbitrates simultaneous multi-axis accelerations so that their $dI/dt$ transients do not compound, and brake choppers protect the inverters from regenerative feedback during emergency stops. \ref{nbk-body-dc-bus-power-integrity} works both halves of that budget, the rail's sag and the stop's regenerative surge, on the mobile manipulator's battery rail.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_pdn_voltage_droop_envelope.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Sustained-load voltage comparison against the 18 V regulator dropout. The 70 A load causes a 4.2 V resistive drop: from 24 V to 19.8 V at full charge, and from 21.5 V to 17.3 V when depleted. This comparison does not establish the transient minimum."}

*The sustained resistive drop fits the rail's headroom at full charge but crosses regulator dropout from a depleted battery. The transient minimum requires separate qualification.*
:::

```{python}
#| label: body-dc-bus-calc
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ BATTERY-RAIL DROOP AND REGENERATIVE SURGE ON THE RUNNING MACHINE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: \ref{nbk-body-dc-bus-power-integrity} in @sec-body-power-integrity.
# │ Goal:    Screen sustained coincident load on the 24 V battery rail and
# │          regenerative voltage during a stop from the drive limit; the
# │          transient minimum requires separate qualification.
# │ Show:    70 A sustained load drops the 24 V rail by 4.2 V to 19.8 V, 1.8 V above
# │          the 18 V regulator dropout at full charge; from the 21.5 V
# │          battery-low point the sustained ohmic term alone crosses it;
# │          75 percent of 414 J regenerated = 310.5 J; capacitor-only endpoint
# │          about 169.7 V; stop lasts 750 ms, so the regenerative peak is
# │          828 W and the chopper resistor <= 1.09 Ohm at a 30 V clamp.
# │ How:     Sustained ohmic screen via calc_voltage_droop with the
# │          machine's rail fields (RM.control_rail_*) and the site transient
# │          (AISLE.i_rail_transient); E_k reused from MachineMomentum.e_k;
# │          capacitor energy balance; triangular power pulse under constant
# │          deceleration a_brake over t_stop = v/a_brake.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import (
    fmt_mass,
    fmt_inductance,
    fmt_capacitance,
    fmt_voltage,
    fmt_current,
    fmt_resistance,
    fmt_power,
    fmt_energy,
    fmt_latency,
    fmt_velocity,
    fmt_acceleration,
    fmt_percent,
    fmt_math,
    fmt_display_math,
    sci_latex,
    check,
)

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class DriveBusIntegrity:
    """Battery-rail droop, regenerative surge, and chopper sizing for the running machine."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    m = RM.loaded_mass  # category: derived (upper bound, full tote rack)
    v = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative (drive limit)
    a_brake = AISLE.a_brake  # category: illustrative (credible deceleration)
    e_k = MachineMomentum.e_k  # category: derived (loaded machine at its drive limit)
    v_bus_nom = RM.control_rail_nominal  # category: chosen (24 V battery rail)
    v_battery_low = RM.control_rail_battery_low  # category: illustrative (depleted battery)
    r_bus = RM.control_rail_resistance  # category: illustrative (harness resistance)
    v_uvlo = RM.control_rail_dropout  # category: illustrative (point-of-load regulator dropout)
    di = AISLE.i_rail_transient  # category: illustrative (inference burst plus drive)
    i_compute = 4.0 * ureg.ampere  # category: illustrative (application processor's share of the step)
    c_bus = 22000.0 * ureg.microfarad  # category: illustrative (bulk link capacitance)
    v_breakdown = 40.0 * volt  # category: illustrative (inverter MOSFET rating)
    regen_fraction = 0.75  # category: illustrative (share of E_k returned to the rail)
    v_clamp = 30.0 * volt  # category: chosen (chopper clamp threshold)
    r_candidate = 1.0 * ureg.ohm  # category: chosen (candidate chopper resistor)
    p_candidate = 1.0 * ureg.kilowatt  # category: chosen (candidate resistor pulse rating)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    i_drive = (di - i_compute).to(ureg.ampere)
    dv_r = calc_voltage_droop(di, r_bus).to(volt)
    dv = dv_r  # sustained resistive drop, not a transient minimum
    v_sustained = (v_bus_nom - dv).to(volt)
    headroom = (v_bus_nom - v_uvlo).to(volt)
    margin = (headroom - dv).to(volt)
    v_sag_low = (v_battery_low - dv_r).to(volt)

    e_regen = (regen_fraction * e_k).to(joule)
    v_final = ((v_bus_nom**2 + 2 * e_regen / c_bus) ** 0.5).to(volt)
    t_stop = (v / a_brake).to(millisecond)
    p_peak = (2 * e_regen / t_stop).to(ureg.watt)
    r_max = (v_clamp**2 / p_peak).to(ureg.ohm)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(dv_r.magnitude - 4.2) < 1e-9, f"Ohmic term must be the canon 4.2 V: {dv_r}")
    check(abs(dv.magnitude - 4.2) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected sustained droop: {dv}")
    check(abs(v_sustained.magnitude - 19.8) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected sustained rail voltage: {v_sustained}")
    check(v_sustained > v_uvlo, "At full charge the sustained-load screen must stay above dropout.")
    check(abs(v_sag_low.magnitude - 17.3) < 1e-9, f"Battery-low ohmic sag must be the canon 17.3 V: {v_sag_low}")
    check(v_sag_low < v_uvlo, "From the battery-low point the ohmic term alone must cross the dropout.")
    check(abs(e_k.magnitude - 414.0) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected kinetic energy: {e_k}")
    check(abs(e_regen.magnitude - 310.5) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected regenerated energy: {e_regen}")
    check(abs(v_final.magnitude - 169.7) < 0.1, f"Unexpected capacitor-only endpoint: {v_final}")
    check(abs(t_stop.magnitude - 750.0) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected stop duration: {t_stop}")
    check(abs(p_peak.magnitude - 828.0) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected regenerative peak: {p_peak}")
    check(
        abs(p_peak.magnitude - (regen_fraction * m * a_brake * v).to(ureg.watt).magnitude) < 1e-6,
        "The triangular-pulse peak must equal the regenerated share of m*a*v.",
    )
    check(abs(r_max.magnitude - 1.0870) < 1e-3, f"Unexpected chopper resistance bound: {r_max}")
    check(r_candidate <= r_max and p_candidate >= p_peak, "The candidate resistor must meet both bounds.")
    check(v_bus_nom < v_clamp < v_breakdown, "The clamp must sit between the rail and the switch rating.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    m_str = fmt_mass(m, unit=kilogram, precision=0)
    v_str = fmt_velocity(v, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    a_brake_str = fmt_acceleration(a_brake, unit=meter / second**2, precision=0)
    v_bus_nom_str = fmt_voltage(v_bus_nom, unit=volt, precision=0)
    v_battery_low_str = fmt_voltage(v_battery_low, unit=volt, precision=1)
    r_bus_str = fmt_resistance(r_bus, unit=ureg.milliohm, precision=0)
    c_bus_str = fmt_capacitance(c_bus, unit=ureg.microfarad, precision=0, commas=True)
    v_uvlo_str = fmt_voltage(v_uvlo, unit=volt, precision=0)
    v_breakdown_str = fmt_voltage(v_breakdown, unit=volt, precision=0)
    i_drive_str = fmt_current(i_drive, unit=ureg.ampere, precision=0)
    i_compute_str = fmt_current(i_compute, unit=ureg.ampere, precision=0)
    di_str = fmt_current(di, unit=ureg.ampere, precision=0)
    dv_display_math = fmt_display_math(rf"\Delta V_{{\text{{sustained}}}} = \Delta I R_{{\text{{bus}}}} = {fmt_voltage(dv, unit=volt, precision=2)}")
    v_sustained_display_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"V_{{\text{{rail, sustained}}}} = {fmt_voltage(v_bus_nom, unit=volt, precision=0)} - {fmt_voltage(dv, unit=volt, precision=2)} = {fmt_voltage(v_sustained, unit=volt, precision=2)}"
    )
    dv_str = fmt_voltage(dv, unit=volt, precision=2)
    v_sustained_str = fmt_voltage(v_sustained, unit=volt, precision=2)
    v_sag_low_str = fmt_voltage(v_sag_low, unit=volt, precision=1)
    headroom_str = fmt_voltage(headroom, unit=volt, precision=0)
    margin_str = fmt_voltage(margin, unit=volt, precision=2)
    e_k_display_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"E_k = \tfrac{{1}}{{2}} m v^2 = \tfrac{{1}}{{2}}\,({m_str})({v_str})^2 = {fmt_energy(e_k, unit=joule, precision=0)}"
    )
    regen_pct_str = fmt_percent(regen_fraction, precision=0, style="prose")
    e_regen_str = fmt_energy(e_regen, unit=joule, precision=1)
    v_final_display_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"V_{{\text{{final}}}} = \sqrt{{V_{{\text{{rail, nom}}}}^2 + \frac{{2 E_{{\text{{regen}}}}}}{{C_{{\text{{bus}}}}}}}} \approx {fmt_voltage(v_final, unit=volt, precision=1)}"
    )
    t_stop_str = fmt_latency(t_stop, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    v_clamp_str = fmt_voltage(v_clamp, unit=volt, precision=0)
    p_peak_display_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"P_{{\text{{regen, peak}}}} \approx \frac{{2 E_{{\text{{regen}}}}}}{{t_{{\text{{stop}}}}}} = {fmt_power(p_peak, unit=ureg.watt, precision=0)}"
    )
    r_max_display_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"R_{{\text{{brake}}}} \le \frac{{V_{{\text{{clamp}}}}^2}}{{P_{{\text{{regen, peak}}}}}} \approx {fmt_resistance(r_max, unit=ureg.ohm, precision=2)}"
    )
    r_max_str = fmt_resistance(r_max, unit=ureg.ohm, precision=2)
    r_candidate_str = fmt_resistance(r_candidate, unit=ureg.ohm, precision=0)
    p_candidate_str = fmt_power(p_candidate, unit=ureg.kilowatt, precision=0)
    p_peak_str = fmt_power(p_peak, unit=ureg.watt, precision=0)
```

::: {#nbk-body-dc-bus-power-integrity .callout-notebook title="DC bus voltage sag and regenerative surge"}
The mobile manipulator's battery feeds one nominal `{python} DriveBusIntegrity.v_bus_nom_str` control rail that carries the drive inverters, the arm's joint drives, and the point-of-load regulators that supply its application processor.

**Problem**: Under the coincident current step of an inference burst and the drive motors, and then a stop from the drive limit, does the rail remain within the operating limits of the regulators and the motor inverters?

**Math**:

1. **Parameters**:
   - Machine mass, travel speed, and credible deceleration: $m =$ `{python} DriveBusIntegrity.m_str` (upper bound, full tote rack), $v =$ `{python} DriveBusIntegrity.v_str`, $a_{\text{brake}} =$ `{python} DriveBusIntegrity.a_brake_str`
   - Rail characteristics: $V_{\text{rail, nom}} =$ `{python} DriveBusIntegrity.v_bus_nom_str`, harness resistance $R_{\text{bus}} =$ `{python} DriveBusIntegrity.r_bus_str`, bulk link capacitance $C_{\text{bus}} =$ `{python} DriveBusIntegrity.c_bus_str`
   - Operating limits: point-of-load regulator dropout $V_{\text{uvlo}} =$ `{python} DriveBusIntegrity.v_uvlo_str`, inverter MOSFET breakdown $V_{\text{breakdown}} =$ `{python} DriveBusIntegrity.v_breakdown_str`
2. **Sustained-load screen**:
   - As an illustrative coincident load, the two drive motors and the arm's joint drives add `{python} DriveBusIntegrity.i_drive_str` while the application processor adds `{python} DriveBusIntegrity.i_compute_str` on the same rail. Their aggregate increase is $\Delta I =$ `{python} DriveBusIntegrity.di_str`. Assume the stated rail voltage is the unloaded source voltage and this coincident demand is the total load in the screen, with no separate compute-rail hold-up.
   - After source current settles to the increased load, the additional resistive drop is:
     `{python} DriveBusIntegrity.dv_display_math`
   - The resulting sustained rail voltage at full charge is:
     `{python} DriveBusIntegrity.v_sustained_display_math`
   - The headroom to the regulators' dropout is `{python} DriveBusIntegrity.headroom_str`, and this `{python} DriveBusIntegrity.dv_str` drop leaves `{python} DriveBusIntegrity.margin_str` of it. This screen does not establish the transient minimum or complete brownout qualification. From the depleted battery, the same sustained drop alone leaves only `{python} DriveBusIntegrity.v_sag_low_str`, below dropout.
3. **Regenerative surge**:
   - During a stop from the drive limit, the loaded machine's kinetic energy must be dissipated:
     `{python} DriveBusIntegrity.e_k_display_math`
   - If the battery management system disconnects charge input and an illustrative `{python} DriveBusIntegrity.regen_pct_str` of kinetic energy returns to the bus ($E_{\text{regen}} =$ `{python} DriveBusIntegrity.e_regen_str`), an unprotected, lossless capacitor-only energy balance would end at:
     `{python} DriveBusIntegrity.v_final_display_math`
   - *Failure mechanism*: Long before the bus reached that endpoint, it would cross the `{python} DriveBusIntegrity.v_breakdown_str` switch rating.
4. **Dynamic braking clamp**:
   - Under deceleration over $t_{\text{stop}} =$ `{python} DriveBusIntegrity.t_stop_str`, regenerative power peaks at `{python} DriveBusIntegrity.p_peak_display_math`
   - To clamp the bus at $V_{\text{clamp}} =$ `{python} DriveBusIntegrity.v_clamp_str` below the switch breakdown rating, the brake chopper must divert this peak power through an absorption resistor:
     `{python} DriveBusIntegrity.r_max_display_math`

**Result**: At full charge the sustained-load screen leaves the rail at `{python} DriveBusIntegrity.v_sustained_str`, only `{python} DriveBusIntegrity.margin_str` above the `{python} DriveBusIntegrity.v_uvlo_str` regulator dropout, so a depleted battery erases the margin. Unbuffered regenerative braking would drive the bus past the `{python} DriveBusIntegrity.v_breakdown_str` MOSFET rating, which calls for a dynamic brake chopper whose resistor is no larger than `{python} DriveBusIntegrity.r_max_str` and absorbs an `{python} DriveBusIntegrity.p_peak_str` peak (satisfied by an illustrative `{python} DriveBusIntegrity.r_candidate_str`, `{python} DriveBusIntegrity.p_candidate_str` component).

**Systems insight**: Mechanical motion and electrical power are bidirectionally coupled. Acceleration requires a supply that sustains the coincident current demand; deceleration requires an adequate absorption or dissipation path. The illustrative chopper meets the modeled peak-power screen, but pulse energy, repetition, cooling, and component tolerances also require qualification.
:::

```{python}
#| label: body-conveyor-freshness-calc
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ FRESHNESS DEADLINE FOR THE MUG ON THE CONVEYOR (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: the freshness item of \ref{chk-body-bus-droop-regen}.
# │ Goal:    Give the moving target the freshness deadline applies to on the
# │          running machine: the mug on the pick-station conveyor.
# │ Show:    0.20 m/s, 15 mm grasp tolerance, 3 mm of it spent by the initial
# │          estimate; the answer (not printed) is (15 - 3) / 0.20 = 60 ms.
# │ How:     Delta t_fresh = e_max / v_max with e_max = r_tol - e_0, from AISLE.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_length, fmt_velocity, check

AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class ConveyorFreshness:
    """Freshness deadline for the mug riding the pick-station conveyor."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    v_conv = AISLE.v_conveyor  # category: illustrative (conveyor speed)
    r_tol = AISLE.grasp_tolerance  # category: chosen (grasp tolerance)
    e_0 = AISLE.grasp_initial_error  # category: illustrative (initial estimate error)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    dt_fresh = ((r_tol - e_0) / v_conv).to(millisecond)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(v_conv.to(meter / second).magnitude - 0.20) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected conveyor speed: {v_conv}")
    check(abs(r_tol.to(ureg.millimeter).magnitude - 15.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected grasp tolerance: {r_tol}")
    check(abs(e_0.to(ureg.millimeter).magnitude - 3.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected initial error: {e_0}")
    check(abs(dt_fresh.magnitude - 60.0) < 1e-9, f"Conveyor freshness deadline must be 60 ms: {dt_fresh}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    v_conv_str = fmt_velocity(v_conv, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    r_tol_str = fmt_length(r_tol, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    e_0_str = fmt_length(e_0, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
```

::: {#chk-body-bus-droop-regen .callout-checkpoint title="The five physical budgets"}

Before measuring these limits on an assembled machine, verify your understanding of the five budgets:

- [ ] **Freshness deadline**: Can you calculate the maximum allowable measurement age for the mug riding the pick-station conveyor at `{python} ConveyorFreshness.v_conv_str`, with a `{python} ConveyorFreshness.r_tol_str` grasp tolerance of which the initial estimate already spends `{python} ConveyorFreshness.e_0_str`, and explain why that age is counted from exposure on the sensor rather than from the start of inference, and why the base's stop for a standing person instead charges age as blind travel?
- [ ] **Velocity ceiling**: Can you explain why doubling the pre-brake delay expands the stopping distance linearly while doubling travel speed expands the braking term quadratically, and why the admissible speed is the positive root of $d_{\text{stop}} \le D_{\text{clear}}$?
- [ ] **Inertia matching**: Can you explain why the gear ratio that maximizes link acceleration makes reflected rotor inertia equal load inertia ($N^2 J_{\text{rotor}} = J_{\text{load}}$), and why oversizing the gearbox for static torque lowers dynamic joint acceleration?
- [ ] **Thermal horizons and runaway**: Can you explain why an actuator can produce three times its rated torque for seconds but destroys its winding insulation if held there for minutes, and how the temperature coefficient of copper ($\alpha_{\text{Cu}}$) turns a sustained stall into runaway?
- [ ] **Rail sag and regeneration**: Can you explain how a coincident compute and drive current step sags a shared rail through resistance, inductance, and capacitor depletion, and why a stop from speed pumps energy back into the bus that a brake chopper must divert?

:::

## Measuring a Machine's Own Limits {#sec-body-measuring-limits}

A brake that stops an unloaded base on a cool laboratory floor has not established how the loaded mobile manipulator stops after repeated maneuvers. Characterization must connect each calculation to measurements under the conditions in which the machine will use it. A dynamometer, a test stand that applies a controlled mechanical load, isolates actuator behavior (@fig-02-real-motor-dyno-bench); integrated trials then establish what changes when the actuator shares a chassis, cooling path, and power supply with the rest of the machine. A defensible limit states what was measured, how uncertain the result is, and which conditions must remain true for a later decision to rely on it.

### Empirical dynamometer characterization and probe intrusion {#sec-body-dynamometer-characterization}

On a dynamometer, a controlled load machine resists the actuator while torque, speed, current, and voltage are measured on a shared timebase. Four tests connect the earlier models to measurable parameters:

- **Torque and back-EMF transduction ($K_t$ and $K_e$)**: By commanding the inverter's Field-Oriented Control (FOC) current loop across a sweep of quadrature phase currents $i_q$ while the dynamometer absorbs torque at constant speed, engineers measure electromechanical torque transduction:
  $$\tau = K_t i_q$$
  Driving the unpowered motor at known speed and measuring open-circuit voltage supplies the corresponding back-EMF constant $K_e = e_{\text{bemf}} / \omega$. These tests establish the conversion factors used in @sec-body-electrical-time-constants.

- **Electrical rise time and inductive bandwidth ($\tau_e = L/R$)**: Under locked-rotor conditions ($\omega = 0$), the dynamometer clamps the output shaft while the inverter applies a step voltage command. The quadrature current step response:
  $$i_q(t) = \frac{V_{\text{bus}}}{R}\left(1 - e^{-t/\tau_e}\right)$$
  reveals the electrical time constant. The current probe and acquisition path must resolve the rise; otherwise the instrument smooths the response being measured and hides the actuator limit.

- **Enclosed thermal resistance ($\theta_{JA}$) and continuous torque ceilings**: A heating trial under the installed cooling conditions measures the winding temperature rise and loss power, establishing $\theta_{JA} = \Delta T / P_{\text{loss}}$. The continuous torque ceiling from @sec-body-thermal-capacity is then:
  $$\tau_{\text{cont}} = K_t \sqrt{\frac{T_{\max} - T_{\text{amb}}}{R(T_{\max}) \theta_{JA}}}$$
  The test must reproduce the enclosure and neighboring heat loads under which that ceiling will be used.

- **Reverse backdrive efficiency ($\eta_{\text{rev}}$) and impact dynamics**: By driving the actuator output shaft with the dynamometer load motor, the testbed measures the reverse backdrive torque threshold:
  $$\tau_{\text{ext}} = \frac{N_g^2 J_{\text{rotor}}}{\eta_{\text{rev}}} \ddot{q} + \frac{\tau_{\text{friction}}}{\eta_{\text{rev}}}$$
  The measured response establishes whether the transmission can yield under the intended external load. Contact qualification must additionally exercise the relevant compliance and impact conditions; the reverse-drive model alone does not predict tooth failure.

::: {#fig-02-real-motor-dyno-bench fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Electric motor dynamometer testbed**: High-bandwidth actuator characterization stand at NASA Armstrong Flight Research Center. Direct empirical measurement of peak torque saturation, electrical time constants ($\tau_e = L/R$), continuous thermal rise ($\Delta T = P_{\text{loss}} \theta_{JA}$), and regenerative power feedback requires synchronizing multi-channel load cells, optical encoders, and isolated current probes on a shared hardware timebase rather than trusting manufacturer catalog ratings.
